newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's lawmakers to choose new heads of Congress. [CORRECTED 21:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Brazil's lawmakers to choose new heads of Congress. [CORRECTED 21:15 GMT]

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to run for re-election faced its second major test this week when Congress was due to choose the new presidents of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

The government hopes candidates from allied parties who back re-election and Cardoso's reform program in general will win the votes scheduled for Tuesday in the Senate and Wednesday in the Chamber of Deputies. (Corrects days when votes are scheduled.)
But analysts said there remained a remote possibility of an upset because voting will be secret and disgruntled members of both houses may seek to rattle the government.
"Things seem to heading the way the government wants, although there will undoubtedly be some level of betrayal by normally allied deputies," said Carlos Lopes of consultants Sante Fe Ideias.
The frontrunner to replace Dep. Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes as president of the Chamber of Deputies is Dep. Michel Temer, the lower house leader of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB).

The government began campaigning on Temer's behalf after he persuaded a large chunk of the PMDB to vote for a constitutional amendment allowing re-election, which was received a first approval in the lower house last week.
Temer also endeared himself to the government last year when he rescued its pension reform bill after an initial draft was rejected by the Chamber of Deputies.

The other two candidates to run the lower house are Dep. Prisco Viana, closely linked to former Sao Paulo mayor and arch anti-reelectionist Paulo Maluf, and Wilson Campos, a rebel member of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB).
A government source in Congress said Temer had enough support to win Tuesday's election outright by gathering more than half the votes of the Chamber's 513 members.
A second round of voting between the two most popular candidates would take place later on Tuesday or perhaps on Wednesday if no one receives an outright majority.
The Senate race pits powerful political boss Sen. Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, one of Cardoso's most important allies from the conservative Liberal Front Party, against Sen. Iris Rezende from the PMDB.
Both candidates support the government's reform program and some Cardoso advisers were until recently reported to favor Rezende as a more reliable ally than the hot-headed Magalhaes.

But Rezende's chances were considered slim after he ordered PDMB deputies not to vote on re-election until after the Senate race, only for the government to win more than half the PMDB's lower house support for re-election.
The PMDB hopes to win both houses to recover some of the political muscle it lost to Cardoso's PSDB and Magalhaes' PFL, the two parties that anchor Brazil's ruling alliance.

But fears the PMDB might seek to defeat the re-election bill once it reaches the Senate if Rezende loses appeared to dissipate after Cardoso publicly pledged his government would not provide behind-the-scenes support to either candidate.

The presidents of both houses, whose terms last two years, are considered key to Cardoso's chances of pressing ahead with his structural reforms mainly because they have the power to speed up or slow down voting procedure.
